llm.summary: This skill appears to be a legitimate ARI Amazon seller tool, but it exposes broader paid, persistent, and account-changing capabilities than its narrow single-ASIN action-plan framing suggests.

dimensions.detail: Network access to the ARI service, API-key use, local file export, and account/business data access are coherent for this product, but the exposed command surface is broader than the advertised action-plan package.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: Setup uses browser authorization or hidden local key entry, stores the ARI API key under the user's home directory with restrictive permissions, uses the standard library, and explicitly warns not to download or run remote update files.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The instructions disclose many safeguards, but they also direct the agent to run some paid report flows without fresh conversational approval when server autoConfirm applies, and the CLI accepts workflow/focus arguments despite the specialized skill saying those values are fixed.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The skill can persist a local API key and can change account-side state such as auto-confirm spending thresholds, recurring schedules, watch records, competitor bindings, alert read state, and review workflow status.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The declared purpose and agent prompt focus on a single-ASIN seller action plan and fixed audit/action workflow, while the artifacts and CLI also expose VOC reports, keyword analysis, competitor comparison, monitoring, exports, category leaderboard, workbench status updates, and account confirmation settings.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Review this before installing if you only expected a narrow action-plan helper. Installing means trusting ARI with an API key and allowing an agent to access seller review data, run paid analyses under account confirmation rules, export data locally, and modify monitoring or workflow state. Set autoconfirm to ask every time if you want per-charge control, avoid using alternate workflow/focus flags, and treat local exports as potentially sensitive business files.
llm.findings:
[LP3] expected: Shell, network, environment-variable key use, and local configuration are expected for this CLI-backed ARI integration, but the package does not provide a separate explicit permissions manifest for those capabilities.
[TP4] unexpected: The broader account, export, monitoring, and paid-analysis functionality is documented in the artifacts, but it materially exceeds the narrow single-ASIN action-plan framing in the front matter and agent prompt.
[SDI-1] unexpected: The CLI and documentation expose a broad seller-operations suite, not only the fixed audit/action workflow promised by skill-defaults.json, _meta.json, README.md, and operation-workflow.md.
[SDI-2] unexpected: Export writes downloaded reviews or reports to a caller-selected local path, and monitoring/account-management commands create lasting state; these are disclosed but overbroad for a specialized action-plan skill.
[EA2] unexpected: The artifacts instruct automatic execution of some credit-consuming VOC/analyze flows when server autoConfirm rules match, and expose an autoconfirm command that changes future spending-confirmation behavior.
[T09] unexpected: The SARIF workflow/focus bypass is supported by the code: operation_payload prefers command-line --workflow and --focus over skill-defaults.json, so a caller can request other server-enabled operation workflows through this specialized package.
[SQP-1] expected: Natural-language invocation and context reuse are part of the intended UX, but with this broad command surface they increase the chance of invoking sensitive actions from casual ASIN-related requests.
[SQP-3] expected: Chinese display text and default prompt match much of the documentation; this is mainly a locale/clarity issue rather than an independent security concern.
